title: Master Hōnen Fabricates the Gate of the Great Vow
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Answer: The so-called “Gate of the Great Vow” is a teaching fabricated by the Japanese master Hōnen (1132–1212), who distorted a passage of Master Shandao's instruction in the Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra.

inline.s: Question: What is the Gate of the Great Vow?
Answer: The so-called “Gate of the Great Vow” is a teaching fabricated by the Japanese master Hōnen (
), who took a passage of Master Shandao's instruction in the Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra, distorted it, and
fabricated this teaching out of it
In the Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra, Master Shandao says:
“Yet the teacher who transforms the Sahā world
(Śākyamuni Buddha)
, because
(of Queen Vaidehī)
requested it, thereupon broadly opened the Essential Gate of the Pure Land; while the Able One of the Land of Peace and Bliss
(Amitābha Buddha)

, reveals the Great Vow of his distinct intent. As for the Essential Gate, it is precisely the two gates of this Contemplation Sutra — the meditative and the non-meditative. The meditative means stilling one's deliberations to concentrate the mind; the non-meditative means abandoning evil to cultivate good. One dedicates these two practices and aspires to be born there. As for the Great Vow, as the Longer Sutra says, all ordinary beings, good or evil, who attain birth, do so without exception by riding upon the power of Amitābha Buddha's great vows and karmic deeds
as
the dominant condition

[Dominant condition] The indirect cause by which any conditioned dharma arises, is brought to completion, or bears fruit. Whatever possesses strong and superior efficacy and can assist another dharma in arising, reaching completion, or bearing fruit is called a dominant condition. For example, sunlight, rain, and the farmer's labor are the dominant conditions for the ripening of seedlings. The Mahāyāna Meaning Chapter says: “A dominant condition is one whose power in producing a dharma is strong; therefore it is called dominant.” [Conditioned dharmas] All things born of the coming together of causes and conditions.
[Cause and condition] When a thing is born, that which directly provides strong power is the cause; that which indirectly adds weaker power is the condition. For example, the seed is the cause,
while sunlight, rain, and the farmer's labor
are the conditions; when these causes and conditions come together, rice grows.

Question: In the Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra, Master Shandao says that the Great Vow is the dominant condition by which all ordinary beings, good or evil, are able to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. This speaks of the condition for rebirth; then what is the cause by which all ordinary beings, good or evil, attain rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss?

Answer: The cause by which all ordinary beings, good or evil, attain rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is what our original teacher Śākyamuni Buddha proclaimed with his golden mouth, and what Amitābha Buddha of the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss praises and embraces — namely, the teaching in
the Sutra in Praise of the Pure Land, the Buddha's Embrace
“Believe and accept, make the vow, and practice as taught.”
Therefore, the Essential Gate is the cause of rebirth, and the Great Vow is the condition of rebirth; only when cause and condition come together can one be reborn — neither may be lacking.
[Believe and accept, make the vow, practice as taught] In the Sutra in Praise of the Pure Land, the Buddha's Embrace, the Buddha says:

“If there are good men or good women of pure faith who hear this inconceivable name of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life with its merits and virtues, and hear of the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss,
they should all believe and accept, make the vow, practice as taught, and be born in that Buddha-land
Please note: “
believe and accept, make the vow, practice as taught, and be born in that Buddha-land
Here Master Shandao is plainly saying that the Great Vow is
the condition for attaining birth in
the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss
— its dominant condition

Yet Master Hōnen distorted this, claiming that in this passage Master Shandao “established three gates: meditative virtue, non-meditative virtue, and the Great Vow” (see The Complete Works of Master Hōnen
Dharma Discourses). In this way he set the Great Vow against the Essential Gate (the meditative and non-meditative virtues), making it a separate gate — this is the so-called Gate of the Great Vow.

As to what the Great Vow is, Master Shandao explains it very clearly: “The Great Vow means, as the Longer Sutra says, that all ordinary beings, good or evil, who attain birth, do so without exception by riding upon the power of Amitābha Buddha's great vows and karmic deeds
as
the dominant condition

.” Thus, in the passage above, Master Shandao is saying that Śākyamuni Buddha, through the Essential Gate (“as for the Essential Gate, it is precisely the two gates of this Contemplation Sutra — the meditative and the non-meditative”), tells beings how to practice so as to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, while Amitābha Buddha welcomes them with his Great Vow. This is what patriarchs and great masters have always called “one sending forth and one welcoming” (Śākyamuni Buddha sends beings forth through the Essential Gate, and Amitābha Buddha
then
welcomes them with his Great Vow). This sending forth and welcoming is a seamless whole — how can it be split apart?

If there were no Śākyamuni Buddha to send beings forth through the Essential Gate (the method of practice for going to the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss), would beings know how to reach the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss? If there were no Amitābha Buddha's Great Vow, could practice of the Essential Gate carry one to the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss? Yet Master Hōnen tore the Essential Gate and the Great Vow apart, setting them side by side as two separate teachings, saying the Essential Gate is Śākyamuni Buddha's teaching and the Gate of the Great Vow is Amitābha Buddha's teaching. He openly declared “two Buddhas, two teachings,” and even demanded “abolishing the Essential and establishing the Great Vow” (abolish the Essential Gate, establish the Gate of the Great Vow), insisting all the while that this was Master Shandao's Pure Land thought
Moreover, this one sending forth and one welcoming is explained with perfect clarity by Master Shandao in the Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra:
Relying wholly upon
(relying wholly upon)
Śākyamuni in this world
sending forth
this shows that
the Essential Gate
is Śākyamuni Buddha's
sending forth
, and Amitābha
thereupon
in that land
comes to welcome
this shows that
the Great Vow
is Amitābha Buddha's
coming to welcome
He calls from there, and this one sends forth —
how could one not go?
Only devote your heart earnestly to upholding the Dharma, for all your life long
, and casting off this defiled body, you will thereupon realize the constant bliss of the Dharma-nature of that land.”

[Relying wholly upon Śākyamuni's sending forth from this world, and Amitābha's coming to welcome from that land] Relying wholly upon Śākyamuni Buddha's sending forth from this world, Amitābha Buddha then comes from that land to welcome. (“yǎng”: to rely upon. “wéi”: solely, only. “jí”: then, thereupon.) Please note
the words “Relying wholly upon Śākyamuni's sending forth from this world, and Amitābha
thereupon
coming to welcome from that land”
— in this sentence the word “
thereupon

” shows that first there is Śākyamuni Buddha's sending forth from this world, and only then does Amitābha Buddha come from that land to welcome. Therefore, the Essential Gate and the Great Vow, this “
sending forth and coming to welcome
is an indivisible whole
In this teaching, Master Shandao is saying: relying wholly upon Śākyamuni Buddha's sending forth from the Sahā world, Amitābha Buddha then comes from the Land of Ultimate Bliss to welcome.
Yet Master Hōnen took this seamless “
sending forth and coming to welcome
“Relying wholly upon Śākyamuni's sending forth from this world
— sending forth
, and Amitābha then in that land
comes to welcome
), forcibly tearing it apart into two opposing teachings (the Essential Gate and the Gate of the Great Vow)
, and even demanded “abolishing the Essential and establishing the Great Vow” (abolish the Essential Gate, establish the Gate of the Great Vow)
, all the while falsely claiming that this was Master Shandao's own judgment and Master Shandao's Pure Land thought.
That such barefaced fraud, such a brazen deception, could have lasted eight hundred years right down to the present day is truly beyond belief!
In this
comment
, Master Shandao especially emphasizes: “
Only
(nothing but)
devote your heart earnestly to upholding the Dharma, for all your life long
(uphold it earnestly for all one's life)
” Here the “Dharma” refers to the practice of the Essential Gate, which one dedicates, aspiring to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss
— this is the cause of rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss,
and therefore it must be upheld earnestly for one's whole life

Master Shandao makes it clear: Amitābha Buddha's Great Vow, in receiving and guiding beings, is the dominant condition for rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, while practicing the Essential Gate and dedicating its merit is the true cause of rebirth there; only when cause and condition come together can one be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Yet Master Hōnen actually tore the Essential Gate and the Great Vow apart, making each a separate gate, and even demanded “abolishing the Essential and establishing the Great Vow” (abolish the Essential Gate, establish the Gate of the Great Vow), insisting all the while that this was Master Shandao's own distinction!
In fact,
Master Shandao,
throughout his entire life,

never once spoke of any “Gate of the Great Vow.” Moreover, so that the great multitude of Buddha-reciters could practice according to the teaching of the Amitābha Sutra, he copied more than a hundred thousand scrolls of the Amitābha Sutra and distributed them to Buddha-reciters (
yet he never once spoke, nor ever wrote, the three characters “Gate of the Great Vow”!

). This amply proves that Master Shandao taught Buddha-reciters to practice according to the teaching of the Amitābha Sutra: with faith and vows, uphold the Name single-mindedly and without confusion. Moved and transformed by him, the fourfold assembly turned their hearts to the Pure Land in numbers beyond counting. Among Master Shandao's disciples, some recited the Amitābha Sutra from a hundred thousand to five hundred thousand times, and some recited the Buddha's name ten thousand to a hundred thousand times a day as their daily practice; of those among them who attained the Buddha-recitation samādhi and accomplished rebirth in the Pure Land, there is no way to record them all. If Master Shandao truly established a “Gate of the Great Vow,” then why did he never once speak of the Gate of the Great Vow, nor ever teach anyone to practice it?

Master Yongming was Amitābha Buddha returned to this world (which is why the seventeenth day of the eleventh lunar month, Master Yongming's birthday, is observed as Amitābha Buddha's holy birthday) — did he ever say
there was any “Gate of the Great Vow”?

Of Master Shandao, Master Yinguang — who was Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva returned to this world — said in praise: “Master Shandao was an emanation of Amitābha, possessed of great spiritual powers and great wisdom. In his grand exposition of the Pure Land he did not esteem the mysterious and subtle, but taught people to cultivate practice in a manner that was genuine, earnest, and down to earth. As for his teaching of the two practices, the exclusive and the mixed, its benefit is boundless.” (Collected Works of Master Yinguang, Letter in Reply to a Certain Layman of Yongjia and His Brothers.) What Master Yinguang praised so highly was precisely “the teaching of the two practices, the exclusive and the mixed — its benefit is boundless” (Master Shandao's instruction on the exclusive and mixed practices). Where did he ever say there was any “Gate of the Great Vow”?

From the time the first patriarch, Master Huiyuan, founded the White Lotus Society more than sixteen hundred years ago, according to the Records of the Sages and Worthies of the Pure Land, the Records of Rebirths Heard in Recent Times, and the Records of Rebirths Seen and Heard in the Present Day, those who knew the time of their departure and passed freely into rebirth are beyond counting — where was there ever any “Gate of the Great Vow”?
In the Sutra in Praise of the Pure Land, the Buddha's Embrace,
the Buddhas of the ten directions

“each display the mark of the broad and long tongue, covering the entire trichiliocosm, surrounding it all around, and speak these sincere words: You sentient beings should all believe and accept this ‘Dharma-gate of praise of the inconceivable merits of the Buddha-land, embraced by all Buddhas’”
. This is to say, the Dharma-gate taught by Śākyamuni Buddha in
the Sutra in Praise of the Pure Land, the Buddha's Embrace
is
praised by the Buddhas of the ten directions as the
Dharma-gate embraced by all Buddhas
How then could there be any “Gate of the Great Vow” standing above this
Dharma-gate embraced by all Buddhas
Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva, who came from the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss to this world, is one who, by “
gathering in the six faculties, and continuing with pure mindfulness
,” gathers Buddha-reciters and brings them back to the Pure Land. Where was there ever any “Gate of the Great Vow” that required “neither keeping the precepts nor practicing”?
From this we can see

that the so-called “Gate of the Great Vow” was fabricated entirely out of thin air by Master Hōnen, and then imposed upon Master Shandao, with the false claim that it is Master Shandao's Pure Land thought (hoisting a great banner as a tiger-skin to wrap around himself, to intimidate and deceive people).
Moreover, in this very Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra, Master Shandao explains
how the Pure Land school is to be practiced
with perfect clarity
and he teaches as follows:

Now, practice is of two kinds: first, the correct practice; second, the miscellaneous practice. What is meant by correct practice is practicing solely in accordance with the sutras of rebirth. What are these?
Single-mindedly
recite and read only this Contemplation Sutra, the Amitābha Sutra, the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, and so on;
single-mindedly
contemplate, observe, and recollect the adornments of the two kinds of reward in that land. If one bows, then
single-mindedly
bow only to that Buddha; if one recites with the mouth, then
single-mindedly
recite only that Buddha's name; if one praises and makes offerings, then
single-mindedly
praise and make offerings only to him — this is called correct. Furthermore, within this correct practice there are two kinds: first,
single-mindedly
reciting only Amitābha's name, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, without regard to how long or short the time,
never abandoning it from thought to thought
— this is called
the act of right assurance

, because it accords with that Buddha's vow; if one relies on bowing, recitation, and the like, these are called the supporting practices. Apart from these two practices, the correct and the supporting, all other good deeds whatsoever are called miscellaneous practices. If one cultivates the foregoing correct and supporting practices, one's mind is ever close to the Buddha,
recollecting him without interruption
, and this is called uninterrupted.”

This is entirely consistent with the teaching of Śākyamuni Buddha in the various sutras, and entirely consistent with the teaching of Master Yongming, who was Amitābha Buddha returned to this world — this is the way of Buddhas being one and the same. Where did he ever say, “
We must abolish Śākyamuni Buddha's teaching and establish Amitābha Buddha's teaching
[Sutras of rebirth] That is, the three Pure Land sutras: the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, the Contemplation Sutra of Immeasurable Life, and the Amitābha Sutra.

[Single-minded] To unify one's mind, keeping the mind's attention on one thing alone. [Right concentration] Correct meditative concentration. When body and mind are pure and free of distraction, it is called “right concentration.” One of the eightfold right path. [Eightfold right path] Also called the eightfold noble path, namely, the eight dharmas of the path of the noble ones. 1. Right view, correct understanding. 2. Right thought, correct reflection. 3. Right speech, proper speech. 4. Right action, proper conduct. 5. Right livelihood, proper occupation or way of life. 6. Right effort, proper endeavor. 7. Right mindfulness, correct awareness. 8. Right concentration, correct meditative concentration. The Amitābha Sutra says: “All these birds, throughout the six periods of day and night, utter harmonious and elegant sounds. Their sounds proclaim the five roots, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment,
the eightfold noble path
, and such dharmas.” [Karma] The activities of body, speech, and mind.
Since Master Hōnen and his followers claim to rely upon Master Shandao, they ought, in accordance with
how the Pure Land school is to be practiced
as taught by him — the
correct and supporting practices (
this is Master Shandao's Pure Land teaching
), to carry it out in a down-to-earth way, and so to teach their disciples and followers. The fact is quite otherwise:
at once lazy and greedy, they abandon the right path and instead resort to fraud and falsehood, deceiving the blind multitude
, so that this erroneous teaching has spread for eight hundred years!

[Lazy and greedy] By lazy is meant unwilling to practice diligently, even fearing diligent practice, vainly hoping to gain without effort; by greedy is meant greed for fame, greed for profit, greed for sensual pleasure, and greed for the fruits of attainment.

In the Buddha Store Sutra, the Buddha told the parable of leading the blind into the pit: In a past age, five hundred blind men were traveling along a road. Coming to a great city, they were exhausted by hunger and thirst. They left one blind man outside the city to watch their belongings, while the rest entered the city to beg for food and drink. Before long, a swindler came to the place where the man kept watch and said, “Hey! Why are you here all alone?” The keeper of the goods answered, “I have many companions; they have all gone into the city to beg for food.” The swindler said, “Do you know, there is a place where a great offering of clothing, food, necklaces, flowers, and all sorts of things is given, to be had as you please. If you want to go, I will take you there.” The keeper answered, “Very well.” The swindler led this blind man away from the place and seized all his belongings. When the other blind men returned after begging food, the swindler said to them, “Did you come upon the great offering assembly?” They answered, “We did not.” The swindler said, “You may put the food you have obtained here, and I will take you to the great offering assembly.” All the blind men left their gains in one place and followed the swindler away. The swindler then led the five hundred blind men to the edge of a great deep pit and said to them, “This ground is level and easy to walk on, and there is a great offering assembly here. You may all turn and walk eastward to receive the offerings.” Thereupon all the blind men at once fell into the pit and died.
Original text:

In a past age, five hundred blind men were traveling along a road. Coming to a great city, they were exhausted by hunger and thirst. They left one blind man outside to watch their goods, while the rest entered the city to beg for food and drink. Before long, a swindler came to the place where the keeper of the goods was and said, “Ho! Why are you here all alone?” The man answered, “I have many companions who have gone into the city to beg for food.” The swindler said, “Do you not know that over there a great offering of clothing, food, necklaces, flowers, and sundry things is given, to be had as you please? If you want them, I will take you there.” The man answered, “Very well.” The swindler led the blind man a little way from the spot and seized all his goods. When the blind men returned after obtaining food, the swindler again said to them, “Did you come upon the great assembly offering?” They answered, “We did not.” The swindler said, “You may put what you have obtained here, and I will take you to the great offering assembly.” All the blind men left their goods together in one place and followed the swindler away. The swindler then brought the five hundred blind men to the brink of a great deep pit and said to them, “This ground is level and good, and there is a great offering assembly here. You may each turn and walk eastward to receive their offerings.” At once they all fell into the pit together and died.

Question: In the Buddhist Door Network interview, Master Jingzong said: “If we look in terms of the Essential Gate and the Great Vow, the thirteen patriarchs can be divided into two kinds: one kind specifically highlights the power of Amitābha's primal vows — for example, Shandao, Daochuo, Tanluan (though Daochuo and Tanluan are not counted among the thirteen patriarchs), Chengyuan, Fazhao, Shaokang, and also Master Yinguang; the others, such as Huiyuan,
Yongming
, Shengchang, Lianchi, Ouyi, Jieliu, Xing'an, and Chewu can all be counted as the Essential Gate.” Is this so?

Answer: This division is utterly absurd. Two points alone suffice to expose it. First, as explained above, the Gate of the Great Vow does not exist at all; it was fabricated by Master Hōnen, so how can one use it as a basis for division? Second, Master Yongming, like Master Shandao, is Amitābha Buddha returned to this world (which is why the seventeenth day of the eleventh lunar month, Master Yongming's birthday, is observed as Amitābha Buddha's holy birthday) — and yet Master Yongming, Amitābha Buddha returned, is actually assigned to the Essential Gate category. Does this not flatly contradict their own theory that “the founder of the Essential Gate is Śākyamuni Buddha, and the founder of the Gate of the Great Vow is Amitābha Buddha”? (From this one can also see how utterly confused is their fabricated theory of the Gate of the Great Vow!)
Among the thirteen patriarchs of the Pure Land school, two were Amitābha Buddha returned to this world: the second patriarch, Master Shandao, and the sixth patriarch, Master Yongming.

These people keep saying that they look up to Master Shandao because Master Shandao is Amitābha Buddha returned to this world; yet they demote Master Yongming, who is likewise Amitābha Buddha returned, to the Essential Gate, and even speak of “abolishing the Essential Gate and establishing the Gate of the Great Vow,”
actually placing Master Yongming, Amitābha Buddha returned, on the list of those to be abolished!
— from this a glimpse can be had of the deviance of the Primal Vow teaching!
These people keep saying that only the seven patriarchs of the three countries are the orthodox line of the Pure Land school. Let me ask:
is the sixth patriarch of the Pure Land school, Master Yongming — Amitābha Buddha returned to this world — not the orthodox line of the Pure Land school?

[Seven patriarchs of the three countries] Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva and Vasubandhu Bodhisattva of India; Masters Tanluan, Chan Master Daochuo, and Master Shandao of China; and the Japanese prelate Genshin and Master Hōnen of Japan — this is the lineage venerated by the Japanese Primal Vow teaching.

These people keep saying that only the seven patriarchs of the three countries are the orthodox line of the Pure Land school, but at bottom what they really want is to elevate Master Hōnen and his followers as the orthodox line of the Pure Land school, and to overturn the lineage of the thirteen patriarchs that begins with Master Huiyuan as first patriarch. Master Hōnen not only forged the Gate of the Great Vow, but also distorted the Sutra in Praise of the Pure Land, the Buddha's Embrace, denying the Dharma-gate embraced by all Buddhas (including, of course, Amitābha Buddha of the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss) (see
Master Hōnen Distorts the Sutra in Praise of the Pure Land, the Buddha's Embrace
). Let me ask: can such a person be the orthodox line of the Pure Land school?
Question: Nowadays some people boast that they are “the purest Pure Land school.” Are they really the purest Pure Land school?
Answer: What they call “the purest Pure Land school” is nothing but a synonym for the teaching system that Master Hōnen fabricated at random — a system at once lazy and greedy (see
The Missteps of Master Hōnen

). It trumpets: recitation of the name guarantees rebirth; there is no need to keep the precepts, no need to cultivate blessings, no need to purify one's own mind, and even a lifetime of wrongdoing does not matter. If one follows this system of theirs to the end, the result will surely be:
The worm on the lion's body feeds on the lion's flesh.
(see
The Practice of Master Hōnen's Teaching
). How can this deserve the word “pure” in any sense?
What they want is to turn the Pure school into a Defiled school!
To turn it into a cesspool that harbors filth and stores uncleanness!
(see
The Practice of Master Hōnen's Teaching

[Worm on the lion's body] A metaphor for the degenerate kind who destroys the Dharma from within. “The worm on the lion's body feeds on the lion's flesh” — this means that monastics who use the Dharma as a tool for gaining fame and profit are not true monastics; they have come to destroy the Buddha-Dharma and to ruin it, and this is the one means by which Māra destroys the Buddha's teaching. When Śākyamuni Buddha was in the world, Māra said he would destroy the Buddha-Dharma, and the Buddha replied, “What I teach is the true Dharma; no one can destroy it.” Māra then said, “In the age of the decline of your Dharma, I will have my descendants all leave home, don the kasāya robe, and destroy your Dharma.” Hearing this, the Buddha shed tears and could do nothing. [Yuān sǒu] A place where fish and beasts gather together.

To teach the Dharma while going against the meaning of the sutras, distorting the scriptural text, and slandering the Buddha and destroying the Dharma — this is impure preaching of the Dharma. The one who preaches the Dharma impurely incurs extremely grave offenses (greater than robbing all beings of the trichiliocosm of their lives), meets with a most fearsome retribution (falling into the great hells), and his followers likewise come to a most pitiable end (entering wrong views from which it is hard to return, they undergo every kind of decline and affliction for hundreds, thousands, myriads of ages, with suffering without end).
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra, though a foe may take one's life
(though a vicious enemy may take a person's life)
, he only destroys one body
(but the life taken is only this one lifetime)
, yet when a foolish person like this preaches the Dharma impurely, he brings great decline and affliction upon beings for thousands, myriads, and millions of kalpas
(because wrong views have entered their minds, his followers cannot shake them off life after life for thousands, myriads, and millions of kalpas, and calamities follow one after another)
. Such a person
(one beguiled by impure preaching of the Dharma)

has his true bodhi-mind obscured and covered by folly, while his cravings blaze up all the more, continuing without interruption. Because of these cravings, he passes back and forth through the five realms, with no good path to tread and no end to birth and death. Therefore, Śāriputra,
the one who preaches the Dharma impurely incurs offenses beyond measure; he also acts as an evil teacher to beings, and slanders the Buddhas of the past, present, and future
. Śāriputra, setting aside the beings of this Jambudvīpa,
even if a person robbed every being of the trichiliocosm of life, the offense of impure preaching of the Dharma is still greater than this
. Why is that? Because such a person destroys the anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas and assists the work of Māra,
and causes beings to undergo every kind of decline and affliction for hundreds, thousands, myriads of lives

, able only to bind and never to release. You should know that such a person is an evil teacher to all beings, and by this false speech he slanders and reviles the Buddhas in the midst of the assembly,
and by reason of these causes and conditions he falls into the great hells
Therefore you should know,
that person would rather cut off his own tongue with a sharp knife than preach the Dharma impurely in the assembly
(Buddha Store Sutra)

[Five realms] The heavens, humans, hells, hungry ghosts, and animals. If one speaks of six realms, then the asuras are added. The reason they are not mentioned here is that the asura realm is subsumed among the realms of the heavens, humans, animals, and hungry ghosts.
